# v3.04-dev

Training Tracker now checks its own configuration when it starts, and rate
limiting by address is more reliable.

## Added

- **A configuration check at startup.** Every setting the application depends on
  used to be read only at the moment something needed it, so a misconfigured
  system looked healthy until the exact wrong thing was attempted — and in two
  cases never looked unhealthy at all.

  Anything missing or malformed is now named in the startup log, with what to set
  and where. In development the check is silent unless there is a problem; in
  production it also prints one line listing the proxy addresses it trusts, which
  is information you cannot get any other way and need in order to check the
  setting below.

## Fixed

- **A missing database address or session secret is now reported plainly at
  startup.** The application previously started normally and then failed with an
  unexplained error the first time somebody tried to sign in — and without a
  session secret it would even let the first-run wizard create an administrator
  account on a system that could never log anyone in.

  Note what this looks like: the service keeps running and the port stays open,
  and only pages and data requests fail. **Do not judge it by the service status
  — read the log**, which now names the setting and what to do.

- **Two silent failures now announce themselves.** Without the encryption key,
  stored mail passwords and authenticator secrets were being written to the
  database unencrypted with nothing said anywhere. Without the scheduling secret,
  automatic backups and scheduled exports were rejected in exactly the same way
  as a forged request, so they never ran and the logs read like a credentials
  problem.

- **Rate limiting by address is materially more reliable.** In several common
  setups every visitor shared a single limit, so one person's failed sign-ins
  could lock out everybody. That case is now detected and reported once.

- **The trusted-proxy list is read properly.** IPv6 addresses match however they
  are written, an address with a port attached is handled, and entries that were
  never supported — network ranges, hostnames — are reported rather than ignored
  in silence.

## Changed

- The documentation now states plainly which proxy misconfiguration the software
  can detect and which it cannot, so the setting gets checked against the real
  network layout rather than assumed correct.

## Upgrading

No action needed. A correctly configured system starts as before, with one extra
line in the log naming the proxy addresses it trusts — worth reading once against
your actual setup. A small number of rate-limit counters reset on the first start
after upgrading; nothing else is affected.
